summary: Year 4 learners identify acute and obtuse angles and compare/order angles up to two right angles by size. Both names are anchored to the right angle: acute is less open than a right angle, obtuse is more open (but less than a straight line, i.e. two right angles). The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering angles when the arm lengths differ — children tend to judge by arm length, enclosed area, or the distance between the tips rather than by the opening. The proposed core teaching move is vertex-on-vertex overlay comparison, with naming intended to follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison rather than preceding it.
misconceptions: Ordering angles by arm length or by the distance between the tips rather than by the opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. list side length, enclosed area and distance between the sides as the irrelevant properties children use)
Judging by the space or area enclosed between the arms rather than the opening
Naming by appearance rather than by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or the two names simply swapped
Naming before comparing: applying acute/obtuse labels without checking against the right angle

activities.title: Order the baited angles, then overlay to check
steps: Receive four angles to drag into order from smallest to largest, where the smallest opening is deliberately drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms.
State out loud, before moving anything, which angle you think is biggest and why.
Overlay any two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned, so only the openings are compared.

Overlay the longest-armed angle on the shortest-armed one and watch the long-armed 'big-looking' angle's opening fall INSIDE the short-armed angle's opening, then compare the other pairs the same way and re-sort all four by opening.
Re-state the rule you now use to decide the order.
activities.insight: An angle's size is its opening, not the length of its arms, the distance between the tips, or the area enclosed. Overlaying vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned isolates the opening, so an angle with longer arms but a narrower opening is seen to be the smaller angle.

activities.title: Sweep a hinge through acute, right and obtuse
steps: Open a hinge or fan slowly from nearly closed to a straight line.

Watch (or control) a label that ticks through acute → right → obtuse as the opening grows, with a small square snapping in at the right angle, and that changes to 'straight line (not obtuse)' when the opening reaches a straight line.
Pause the sweep and name the zone the opening is currently in.
Identify where obtuse stops — at a straight line, which equals two right angles.
activities.insight: The names acute, right and obtuse are zones of openness defined relative to the right-angle benchmark: acute is less open than a right angle, right is exactly a right angle, and obtuse is more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

activities.title: Hunt and colour-sort angles inside shapes
steps: Examine a given triangle or convex quadrilateral (one with no inside angle more open than a straight line).
Find every angle and decide whether it is acute, right or obtuse by comparing each to a right angle.
Colour-sort the angles by type (e.g. one colour for acute, one for right, one for obtuse).
Explain, for a tricky angle, how you checked it against the right angle rather than guessing from its appearance.
activities.insight: Acute, right and obtuse angles occur inside real shapes, and each is classified by comparison to a right angle — not by the orientation of the shape or the length of its sides.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: short wide angle vs long narrow angle
steps: Look at two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening.
Predict which is the bigger angle and say why, before anything is moved.
Overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's.
Reconcile your prediction with what the overlay shows, and restate the rule for comparing angles.
Answer the probe: if the long arms were made much shorter, would the angle's place in the order change? Why? And could a short-armed angle ever be bigger than a long-armed one — can you draw one?
activities.insight: The reason a learner gives first is the diagnostic part: a learner who predicts B is bigger 'because its lines are longer' is asked to reconcile that with the wider opening of A winning once the angles are overlaid.

checkQuestion: Give the child four angles to order from smallest to largest, with arm length deliberately anti-correlated with opening — the smallest opening is drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms. Say: 'Put these four angles in order, from the smallest angle to the biggest.' Then: 'Tell me how you decided the order.'
checkAnswer: Orders the angles by their opening, ignoring arm length (so the long-armed narrow angle goes first and the short-armed wide angle last), and justifies by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each to a right angle — not by how long the lines are.
